recap_lines: A probability can be a count, a long-run frequency, or a belief that updates.
A chain multiplies conditionals, and assuming independence overstates it.
Bayes' theorem turns a prior and a likelihood into a posterior.
When the base rate is low, most flags from a good test are false positives.
Calibration, unlike accuracy, asks whether stated confidence matches outcomes.
Distribution shift and heavy-tailed loss can break a number that once held.
bookends.command: Quiz me on the terms for judging a confident number. Give me one short case at a time. I must name the exact term, choosing from base rate, sensitivity, PPV, which is positive predictive value, calibration, overconfidence, decorative number, independence, the multiplication rule, distribution shift and heavy-tailed. I must also say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then correct me briefly.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Many people believe a confident number tells you how sure to be. A model says ninety-nine percent, so you trust it ninety-nine percent. But the stated number and what happens are different things. A confident number has to be checked against what happened. This film goes through thirty-three terms for making that check, each one shown in a picture.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. A probability can be a count, a long-run frequency, or a belief that updates. A chain multiplies conditionals, and assuming independence overstates it. Bayes' theorem turns a prior and a likelihood into a posterior. When the base rate is low, most flags from a good test are false positives. Calibration, unlike accuracy, asks whether stated confidence matches outcomes. Distribution shift and heavy-tailed loss can break a number that once held.
